🚨 Hiring | Actuarial Forecasting Lead (C2H) | Remote 🚨

📌 Role: Actuarial Forecasting Lead
📍 Location: Remote – USA
📄 Duration: 12 Months (C2H)
🚀 Start Date: ASAP

We are seeking an experienced Actuarial Forecasting Lead with 12–15 years of experience in actuarial forecasting, claims modeling, and insurance analytics. The ideal candidate will have expertise in claims behavior, loss development, actuarial modeling, and financial forecasting for insurance and protection products. This role requires close collaboration with actuarial, finance, claims, data science, and technology teams to improve forecasting accuracy and support business planning.


Required Skills & Experience
✔ 12–15 years of actuarial forecasting and modeling experience
✔ Strong expertise in actuarial modeling, claims frequency & severity analysis, loss ratio projections, and claims cost estimation
✔ Experience with claims reserving, loss development analysis, and ultimate loss projections
✔ Hands-on experience building and validating actuarial forecasting models using historical claims data, exposure data, and cost assumptions
✔ Knowledge of extended warranty, device protection, service contracts, or specialty insurance products
✔ Understanding of repair & replacement costs, product failure patterns, and claim incidence rates
✔ Experience with actuarial and statistical modeling tools
✔ Exposure to predictive analytics, AI/ML techniques, and actuarial forecasting models
✔ Experience collaborating with actuarial, underwriting, finance, claims, supply chain, and engineering teams

Key Responsibilities
🔹 Review and enhance actuarial forecasting models, methodologies, and assumptions
🔹 Analyze historical claims, failure rates, repair/replacement trends, and product behavior
🔹 Improve forecasting accuracy through statistical, actuarial, and predictive modeling techniques
🔹 Validate models using back-testing, scenario analysis, and actual-vs-expected comparisons
🔹 Partner with actuarial, supply chain, data science, and engineering teams to align forecasting with business planning
🔹 Lead model validation, functional discussions, and business acceptance activities

Qualifications
🎓 Bachelor's or Master's degree in Actuarial Science, Statistics, Mathematics, or a related quantitative field
🎓 Actuarial certification (or progress toward certification) is a plus but not mandatory
🎓 Proven experience applying actuarial projections to claims forecasting and business planning

📩 Interested candidates, please share your updated resume at: Divyanshu@linktms.com

英伟达 has hired the former head of data centers at OpenAI to help lead its DSX platform team. The move is not about software. It is about the physical layer underneath the software: how AI factories are designed, powered, cooled and connected to the grid.

That admission matters. For three years, the AI narrative was a chip story. The bottleneck was compute. Nvidia's job was to ship faster GPUs. The data center was someone else's problem, usually a utility's. That era is ending. A single AI factory can draw hundreds of megawatts, and the companies building them are discovering that the grid interconnection queue is longer than their product cycle. The constraint has moved from silicon to electrons.

DSX is Nvidia's answer. It is a reference design for how to build an AI factory as a unified system, not a collection of procurement decisions. Cooling, power delivery, rack density, on-site generation, grid interaction. These are no longer facilities details. They are architectural variables that determine whether a cluster can be deployed at all. Hiring someone who ran OpenAI's data center buildout is a signal that 𝗡𝘃𝗶𝗱𝗶𝗮 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗻𝗱𝘀 𝘁𝗼 𝗼𝘄𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗮𝗿𝗰𝗵𝗶𝘁𝗲𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲, 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗷𝘂𝘀𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗰𝗵𝗶𝗽𝘀 𝗶𝗻𝘀𝗶𝗱𝗲 𝗶𝘁.

The convergence is already visible across the industry. Google signed a 1 GW virtual power plant deal with Voltus to make its data centers dispatchable. 微软 contracted nuclear restarts and uprates. Meta is funding gas plants in Louisiana and solar in Texas. 西门子能源, GE Vernova and Mitsubishi Heavy Industries are selling turbine backlogs into 2030. 𝗘𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘆 𝗵𝘆𝗽𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗰𝗮𝗹𝗲𝗿 𝗶𝘀 𝗯𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗮𝗻 𝗲𝗻𝗲𝗿𝗴𝘆 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗽𝗮𝗻𝘆, whether it wants to admit it or not.

StarCharge operates in this integration layer, where power, storage and load management must behave as one system from the first day of operation. A data center with on-site storage and grid-interactive controls is not a passive load waiting for a utility upgrade. It is a flexible asset that can be energised on a timeline the compute roadmap requires, not the one the interconnection queue allows.

Nvidia did not just make a hire. It acknowledged that the next phase of AI will be won by whoever can deliver power, not just performance.

AI can help build a shortlist. People still need to own the hiring decision.
ICIMS and Aptitude Research's 2026 research highlights a practical challenge: AI is becoming part of recruiting workflows, while transparency and governance still need attention.
For full-time and contract staffing, I would put three checks around AI-assisted hiring:
1. Set clear criteria before screening.
Agree on the skills and outcomes the role requires. Keep the assessment relevant to the work.
2. Verify the evidence.
Review AI-generated summaries against the candidate's actual experience. Use structured conversations and practical examples to understand how they approach the job.
3. Keep a person accountable.
A recruiter or hiring manager should be able to explain the decision, question a recommendation and correct an error.
For permanent roles, look at long-term ownership and growth. For contract roles, validate the specific deliverables and readiness for the assignment.
My view: use the time saved on administration to improve the quality of the conversation and the decision.
Where is AI most useful in your hiring process today, and where do you keep human review essential?
Source: ICIMS and Aptitude Research, April 2026

Claude spends about 80% of an interactive session waiting for a human.

Anthropic published a report on how AI changed work inside Anthropic. Based on what people actually do, not what they say: agent logs, commits, calendars, hiring records.

1. Fewer juniors
Juniors among new technical hires: 27% → 9% since early 2025. And the company tripled in size. So as I read it, not layoffs. Demand is changing shape.

2. Agents work more hours than people
Agent hours passed human hours in March 2026. By August, employees' agents worked 6 times as many hours as the people. That's not six replaced employees. But the scale is impressive.

3. Output is up
Commits per engineer about 5x in six months. More deals, contracts, invoices. But 5x commits is not 5x value.

4. People are the bottleneck
That 80% blew my mind. Non-technical teams would need over half a work week just to read Claude's output. Meta-work (specs for agents, agents reviewing agents, monitoring) grew from 10% to 22% of Claude sessions between fall 2025 and spring 2026. We're all managers of AI agents now 😁

5. MORE meetings
The median employee meets 20% more than a year ago. Part is company growth, but technical people who manage nobody also meet 16% more. My guess: code got easy. Agreeing, deciding and owning it didn't.

6. A different kind of employee
Hiring managers put more weight on autonomy and judgment, less on narrow expertise. About 17 engineers per PM, and commits from managers in technical teams doubled. Just coordinating isn't enough anymore.

AI was supposed to free us from work. So far it frees us from doing the work and leaves us managing it.

Anthropic is a special company, of course. You can't copy its results onto the whole economy.
